title: The Measurement That Arrives Late: Fusing What Is Already Old

questions.question: A camera fix is 300 ms old by the time your filter sees it. You fuse it as though it described the present. What happens to the estimate?
options: It becomes noisier but stays centred on the truth
It is dragged back into the measurement's past, and trails the truth by roughly the distance travelled during the delay
It improves, since any absolute fix beats dead reckoning
It is unaffected, because the filter averages many fixes
questions.explanation: Measured at 1 m/s: 0.0325 m error with a current fix, 0.2930 m with one 300 ms old. At 600 ms it was 0.5920 m, worse than the 0.4478 m of dead reckoning alone.

questions.question: What does projecting the measurement forward before fusing require, and what does it cost?
options: Nothing, since the timestamp alone is enough
A second filter running in parallel
The motion accumulated since the moment it describes, which the filter already has
Re-running the whole filter from the start
questions.explanation: A ring of doubles as deep as the longest latency. Projected forward, the error went from 0.0325 m at no latency to 0.0494 m at 600 ms, against 0.5920 m for the naive fusion.

questions.question: You rewind the filter to the measurement's moment, correct there, and replay the motion since. Why was that measured as worse than projecting forward at 300 ms?
options: It is not worse; the measurement must be mistaken
Floating point error accumulates over the replay
Rewinding loses the variance
It replays the motion but not the corrections
questions.explanation: A rewind reaching further back than the fix interval discards the corrections in between. Up to 80 ms it matched the projection exactly. From 150 ms it was worse, and fixes arrived every 100 ms. Rewinding is the textbook answer and it is exact only if you replay everything, corrections included.

questions.question: Across fix ages from 0 to 600 ms the actual error went from 0.0325 m to 0.5920 m. What did the filter report as its own deviation?
options: 0.0376 m in every case: a variance is a statement about the model, not about the answer
It became infinite once the filter diverged
It grew with the latency, tracking the actual error
It grew, but understated the error by about half
questions.explanation: Nothing was wrong with the arithmetic. It was answering a different question: given these variances and this motion model, how uncertain should I be? Late measurements are not in that question.

questions.question: An innovation monitor watches the residuals. At a steady 1 m/s it reported 0.921, 0.923, 0.927 and 0.935 for fix ages of 0, 80, 300 and 600 ms. Why did it see nothing?
options: The monitor needs more samples to converge
The estimate had been dragged into the measurement's past
The normalisation divided the error away
The residuals were too small to measure
questions.explanation: The two agreed with each other while both disagreed with the world. An innovation compares the measurement against the prediction, and both were wrong in the same way. Under stop and go the same runs gave 0.921, 1.182, 2.679 and 4.386.

questions.question: What follows for how you run an acceptance test?
options: It should be repeated until the monitor converges to exactly 1.0
It should hold every condition constant so the numbers are repeatable
It should be run at the robot's maximum speed for the longest possible time
It must include acceleration, stops and turns, since a consistency check is blind to any error that does not change
questions.explanation: A steady state hides every error proportional to a rate of change, and that goes well beyond estimation. The monitor is also a change detector, so compare it against its own healthy baseline rather than against a theoretical 1.0: these runs sat at 0.921 when everything was right.
